questions.question: Three overlapping circles inside a rectangle divide the sample space into:
options: Six regions
Eight regions
Three regions
Nine regions

questions.question: If a question says '15 play soccer AND athletics' (no 'only'), the exactly-two region gets:
options: 15 minus the centre count, because the and-count includes those playing all three
15, straight in
15 plus the centre count
Half of 15

questions.question: In the survey of 150 learners, the number playing NO sport is:
P(a random learner plays at least two codes) equals:
Drawing without replacement means the second-stage branches must:
options: Repeat the first-stage probabilities exactly
Be conditioned on which branch you sit on — the remaining sweets have changed
Always be equal to a half
Use the original denominator of 5

questions.question: With 3 red and 2 blue sweets drawn without replacement, P(red then red) is:
P(one sweet of each colour) is found by:
options: Adding the two qualifying paths: 6/20 + 6/20 = 3/5
Multiplying the two qualifying paths together
Taking 1 minus P(red then red)
Averaging P(red) and P(blue)

questions.question: The audit for any completed tree diagram is:
options: Every branch must equal a half
The longest path must be the most likely
The number of paths must equal the number of sweets
All path products must sum to exactly 1

questions.question: In the 200-learner table, P(a random learner is a boy who walks) is:
Marginal probabilities such as P(boy) are read from:
options: The centre cell of the table
The largest cell in the row
The row and column totals in the margins
The grand total divided by four

questions.question: Gender and transport are independent in the original table because:
options: P(boy) × P(walk) = 0,4 × 0,375 = 0,15, exactly matching the cell probability
Boys and girls have equal totals
The table has two rows and two columns
More learners ride taxis than walk

questions.question: Another sign of that independence inside the numbers is:
options: The grand total is exactly 200
Walkers are outnumbered by taxi riders in both rows
The margins are all multiples of 5
The walking rate is 37,5% among boys AND 37,5% among girls — the rows tell one story

subtopics.title: Choosing the Tool and Mixing the Rules

questions.question: Sequence language — 'first', 'then', 'without replacement' — calls for:
options: A contingency table
A tree diagram
A three-circle Venn diagram
The complement rule only

questions.question: A population classified by two characteristics — like gender and transport — calls for:
options: A tree diagram with four branches
A single circle
A contingency table with margins
A frequency polygon

questions.question: Rain has probability 0,3; the team wins with 0,4 if it rains and 0,65 if dry. P(win) is:
That weather calculation uses the tree rules:
options: Add along each path, then multiply the paths
Multiply all four numbers given
Subtract the smaller path from the larger
Multiply along each path, then add the paths where the team wins

subtopics.title: Eight Rooms, Filled from the Middle

questions.question: In the house picture, the middle room is filled first because:
options: It is the biggest room in the house
Its number is the only one that always arrives clean, needing no interpretation
The outside stoep depends on it directly
It is closest to the front door

questions.question: The word that decides whether to subtract the middle room from a shared-room count is:
options: 'And' on its own
'Neither'
'Only' or 'but not'
'At least'

questions.question: The 35 learners on the stoep represent:
options: Those who play exactly one sport
Those who play all three sports
The netball-only players
Those who play no sport at all

questions.question: 'Exactly one code' is answered by pointing at:
options: The three loyal single-sport rooms: 77 of 150
The middle room only
Every room including the stoep
The three shared rooms

questions.question: 'The packet remembers' means:
options: The sweets are always drawn in colour order
Red sweets are drawn more often than blue
Each draw changes the world the next draw faces — the events are dependent
The first draw has no effect on the second

questions.question: Following one path of the tree — red THEN red — is:
options: An or-story, so the probabilities add
An and-story, so the probabilities multiply
A complement, so subtract from 1
Independent, so the branches are equal

questions.question: After a blue sweet is eaten first, the second draw's branches are:
options: 3/5 red and 2/5 blue
2/4 red and 2/4 blue
1/4 red and 3/4 blue
3/4 red and 1/4 blue

questions.question: The 'receipt' at the end of every tree question is:
options: Adding all path products and confirming they total exactly 1
Counting that the tree has exactly four branches
Checking the first-stage probabilities are equal
Multiplying all path products together

subtopics.title: The Register at the School Gate

questions.question: In the register picture, independence between gender and transport means:
options: Boys and girls are equal in number
The rows tell the same story — walking rates match across genders
Every cell of the table is equal
Nobody walks to school

questions.question: In the original register, the walking rate among boys is 30 out of 80, which is:
In the tilted data — 40 of 80 boys walking against 35 of 120 girls — the verdict becomes:
options: Dependent: the rows split apart, 50% against about 29%, and the product test fails
Independent, because the walk total is still 75
Mutually exclusive
Impossible to judge from a table

questions.question: A complete answer to a table independence question ends with:
options: The grand total, circled
A redrawn version of the table
The percentages only, no conclusion
A written sentence giving the verdict with both compared numbers in it
